question: Your public API serves a mobile app and a web client. Mobile needs 3 fields from User, while web — a full profile with orders and statistics. Which API style best solves this problem?

options.text: REST with query parameter ?fields=name,email
options.explanation: Sparse fieldsets (fields filtering) is a partial solution, but it doesn't cover nested resources (posts with comments). GraphQL does this natively with schema-based typing

options.text: gRPC — binary protocol is the fastest
options.explanation: gRPC is not natively supported by browsers (requires a gRPC-Web proxy). It's ideal for inter-service communication, but for a public API with mobile/web clients — not the best choice

options.text: REST with different endpoints for mobile and web clients
options.explanation: Creating separate REST endpoints for each client leads to code duplication and API bloat. This is essentially a manual implementation of what GraphQL does out of the box

options.text: GraphQL — client requests exactly the fields it needs
options.explanation: GraphQL solves the overfetching problem (mobile gets only 3 fields) and underfetching (web gets everything in one request). Each client forms its own query, and the schema is shared

question: Why is cursor-based pagination better than offset-based for a news feed?

options.text: This requires a special license
options.explanation: The listed technologies have open-source versions.

options.text: Can jump to an arbitrary page (e.g., directly to page 50)
options.explanation: Actually — this is a drawback of cursor pagination. Cursor only allows next/prev, without arbitrary jumps. Offset works well for admin panels with page numbers

options.text: No duplicates or skips when new entries are added between page requests
options.explanation: Cursor is tied to a specific element (WHERE id < cursor). New entries at the top don't shift the position. With offset, a new post shifts all offsets — a user may see the same post twice

options.text: O(1) performance instead of O(offset) — equally fast on any page
options.explanation: SQL OFFSET 100000 scans and skips 100000 rows. Cursor (WHERE id < 12345 LIMIT 20) uses an index — always fast, even on page 5000

options.text: Cursor can be used as a stable bookmark to save the user's position
options.explanation: A cursor is a unique pointer to a position in the list. You can save the cursor and return to the same spot. Offset breaks if the data has changed

question: Which rate limiting algorithm is best for an API that requires: even request flow with controlled bursts?

options.text: Sliding Window Log — the most accurate
options.explanation: Sliding Window Log is accurate, but requires O(N) memory (stores the timestamp of every request). It doesn't have a separate burst parameter — it only controls the total number of requests in the window. For steady flow with bursts, Token Bucket is simpler and more effective

options.text: Leaky Bucket — guarantees an even flow
options.explanation: Leaky Bucket provides an absolutely even flow without bursts (fixed drain rate). This is good for some cases, but the question requires controlled bursts — and Leaky Bucket eliminates them entirely

options.text: Token Bucket — controlled burst via the burst parameter, even rate via the rate parameter
options.explanation: Token Bucket is a perfect fit: rate sets the steady replenishment speed, burst sets the maximum spike. O(1) memory. This is the most popular algorithm (used in nginx, AWS API Gateway, Stripe)

options.text: Fixed Window — simple and predictable
options.explanation: Fixed Window has a serious problem at window boundaries: a client can send 2x the limit in a short window (100 requests at the end of window 1 + 100 at the start of window 2). This is exactly an uncontrolled burst

question: You're building a payment API. The client sends POST /payments, gets a timeout, and retries. How to prevent double charging?

options.text: Use a unique orderId and check for duplicates in the database
options.explanation: Checking orderId in the database is a partial solution. But what if the first request is still in-flight and the retry has already arrived? You need a locking mechanism (mutex/lock) on the idempotency key, not just a database check. The full Idempotency-Key pattern accounts for this

options.text: Check on the client side whether the payment went through before retrying
options.explanation: The client received a timeout — it doesn't know if the payment went through. GET /payments?orderId=X may return an empty result even if the payment is in progress. Race condition. Idempotency key solves the problem on the server

options.text: Use PUT instead of POST — PUT is idempotent by specification
options.explanation: PUT is idempotent, but it replaces the entire resource. Creating a payment is a POST (creating a new resource). Semantically, PUT doesn't fit. Moreover, PUT idempotency is not guaranteed automatically — it must be implemented

options.text: Make POST /payments idempotent via Idempotency-Key in the header
options.explanation: The client generates a unique Idempotency-Key (UUID) and sends it with every request. On the first request, the server executes the operation and saves the result. On retry with the same key — it returns the saved result without re-executing. This is the standard (Stripe, PayPal)

question: Which statements about API versioning strategies are correct?

options.text: Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json) keeps URLs clean
options.explanation: Header versioning doesn't pollute URLs and follows the HTTP content negotiation principle. Drawback: harder to test (can't just open the URL in a browser), requires a specific client

options.text: When releasing a new version, the old one can be turned off immediately
options.explanation: No! Clients depend on the old version. Best practice: Deprecation notice 6–12 months in advance, Sunset and Deprecation headers, monitoring traffic to the old version, supporting at least 2 versions simultaneously

options.text: URL path versioning (/v1/users) — the most obvious and popular approach
options.explanation: URL versioning is used by most public APIs (Stripe /v1, Twitter /2, GitHub /v3). Obvious for developers, easy to route at the API Gateway level, convenient for browser testing

options.text: Better not to version at all — make only backward-compatible changes
options.explanation: This is the ideal, but in practice it's impossible to avoid breaking changes indefinitely. Sometimes you need to rename fields, change formats, or remove deprecated features. Without versioning, you limit API evolution
